figures.title: McHugh Mission chair, branded rail.
figures.alt: Oak armchair with straight posts and a branded front rail.
figures.caption: The word Mission starts as a New York brand, not as a California inventory.

figures.title: The Popular Shop, Fifth Avenue exterior or a period interior advertisement.
figures.alt: A late-nineteenth-century New York shopfront or furnished room.
figures.caption: McHugh sold rooms. The oak line was one product inside a decorator’s business.

figures.title: *The Craftsman*, vol. 1, no. 1, October 1901, cover.
figures.alt: Magazine cover dated October 1901.
figures.caption: Stickley’s word was Craftsman. He printed it monthly.

figures.title: Gustav Stickley armchair, oak, about 1903.
figures.alt: Oak armchair with leather seat and visible joinery.
figures.caption: A shop number is not a synonym for Mission.

figures.title: Swedenborgian Church, San Francisco, interior looking toward the chancel.
figures.alt: Shingled church interior with beams and simple chairs.
figures.caption: The chairs McHugh thought were “mission” were made for this church.

figures.title: Grand Rapids “Mission” suite in a trade-paper cut, about 1906–10.
figures.alt: Catalog page of a matching oak parlor suite.
figures.caption: Once the name sold, a factory could add a page.

figures.title: Title page, *The Stones of Venice*, an American edition.
figures.alt: Nineteenth-century title page naming Ruskin and Venice.
figures.caption: The American movement begins with a book, not with a tenon.

figures.title: Society of Arts and Crafts, Boston, early exhibition catalog or mark.
figures.alt: Catalog cover or society emblem, late 1890s.
figures.caption: 1897, before *The Craftsman*. A jury, not a factory.

figures.title: Irene Sargent, portrait or *Craftsman* masthead with her essay title.
figures.alt: Magazine page with Sargent’s byline.
figures.caption: She taught Stickley’s readers how to say Gothic without living in Venice.

figures.title: United Crafts or Craftsman Workshops mark, burned or paper label.
figures.alt: Shop mark on oak.
figures.caption: A guild word on a factory product.
figures.license: object PD photograph or museum CC0.

figures.title: A Boston society chair or cabinet, not a Stickley.
figures.alt: Arts and Crafts cabinet with a documented Boston maker.
figures.caption: The phrase Arts and Crafts had furniture before Eastwood standardized the slat.

figures.title: Title page, *Hints on Household Taste*, Boston: James R. Osgood, 1872.
figures.alt: 1872 Boston title page naming Eastlake and Osgood.
figures.caption: The American Eastlake problem starts as a book, not as a slat.

figures.title: Plate of a table or cabinet from the Osgood *Hints*.
figures.alt: Wood-engraved furniture plate with incised Gothic detail.
figures.caption: Factories traced the grammar. They did not need the author’s permission.

figures.title: American factory “Eastlake” parlor table, walnut or cherry, incised skirt, about 1875–85.
figures.alt: Dark parlor table with incised geometric lines and a lower shelf.
figures.caption: This is what the name meant in a Midwestern parlor. It is not Mission.

figures.title: Kimbel and Cabus desk, oak, about 1875.
figures.alt: Modern Gothic oak desk with trestle feet and strap hardware.
figures.caption: A New York shop that read the English plates and still signed the work.

figures.title: Kimbel and Cabus trade-catalog photograph of Modern Gothic stock, 1870s.
figures.alt: Period photograph of an ebonized cabinet with incised gilt lines.
figures.caption: Once a grammar can be photographed, a factory can copy it.

figures.title: Japanese Dwelling, Fairmount Park, 1876.
figures.alt: Wooden Japanese house on the exhibition grounds with visitors.
figures.caption: Cabinetmakers could walk into the joinery. They did not have to imagine it.

figures.title: Japanese Bazaar, 1876.
figures.alt: Japanese bazaar building with a crowd and sale goods.
figures.caption: The other Japanese building was a shop.

figures.title: Japanese court in the Main Exhibition Building.
figures.alt: Hall interior with lacquer, bronzes, and screens.
figures.caption: Seven thousand packages. A pencil in a joiner’s pocket.

figures.title: Collinson and Lock drawing-room installation, Philadelphia, 1876.
figures.alt: British art-furniture room with ebonized cabinets.
figures.caption: Godwin, Talbert, Batley — a stand, not a guild.

figures.title: Kimbel and Cabus Modern Gothic cabinet, the sort shown in 1876.
figures.alt: Ebonized or oak Gothic cabinet with strap hinges.
figures.caption: New York had the grammar before the fair advertised it.

figures.title: Machinery Hall or an American factory furniture aisle, 1876.
figures.alt: Long exhibition hall of ornate American suites.
figures.caption: Most of the fair was still walnut the trade already knew.

figures.title: Napoleon Sarony photograph of Wilde, New York, 1882.
figures.alt: Wilde standing, fur-trimmed coat, 1882 studio portrait.
figures.caption: The costume the papers came for. The talk was longer than the coat.

figures.title: Chickering Hall, exterior or a period concert bill.
figures.alt: A Fifth Avenue concert hall.
figures.caption: 9 January 1882. A dated room, not an influence fog.

figures.title: A newspaper woodcut of the Leadville visit.
figures.alt: Wilde among miners, period cartoon or sketch.
figures.caption: Check the paper. The Cellini story travels; the hall is the fact.

figures.title: American parlor, c. 1882, still Eastlake.
figures.alt: Rectilinear parlor table in a crowded room.
figures.caption: What the audience walked home to.

figures.title: *House Beautiful* magazine, an early Chicago cover (1896 or after).
figures.alt: Magazine cover using the phrase House Beautiful.
figures.caption: The phrase became American property. It is not a Wilde furniture line.

figures.title: McHugh Mission low-down chair, branded rail.
figures.alt: Oak armchair with straight posts and a manufacturer’s brand under the rail.
figures.caption: The 1993 Utica platform let the New York letters speak.

figures.title: The Popular Shop, Fifth Avenue and 42nd Street, exterior or a period interior advertisement.
figures.alt: Late-nineteenth-century New York shopfront or furnished room.
figures.caption: A decorator’s address, later across from the Library.

figures.title: Walter J. H. Dudley, dimensioned furniture drawing for Jos. P. McHugh & Co., ca. 1903–15.
figures.alt: Pencil drawing of a chair or stand with measurements and a client line.
figures.caption: The Mission line had a draughtsman. The sheets still carry addresses.

figures.title: McHugh Mission magazine stand with X-brace, or a Wanamaker-sold example.
figures.alt: Oak stand with a characteristic X in the back.
figures.caption: A decorator’s shape, later sold in a department store.

figures.title: New York Building interior, Pan-American Exposition, Buffalo, 1901, with McHugh furniture if a photograph survives.
figures.alt: Fair interior with oak furniture in a state building.
figures.caption: Eight million tickets. The trade papers filled afterward.

figures.title: 1906 advertisement, “McHugh Mission Style.”
figures.alt: Magazine advertisement using McHugh Mission Style as a house phrase.
figures.caption: By 1906 the adjective was treated as a trademark.

figures.title: Swedenborgian Church sanctuary, looking toward the hearth, with Forbes chairs in place.
figures.alt: Shingled church interior with madrone trunks and rows of simple maple chairs.
figures.caption: Church chairs. Not a Spanish sacristy.

figures.title: A. J. Forbes side chair, maple and rush, after the 1894 church design.
figures.alt: Straight maple side chair with a woven rush seat and flared feet.
figures.caption: The pattern could be repeated. It was still not oak.

figures.title: Lyon Street portico, Mission clay tiles and brick arches.
figures.alt: Arched stucco-and-brick entrance with a tiled shed roof.
figures.caption: The tiles are an architectural quotation. They are not a factory.

figures.title: A. Page Brown specification page or the 20 August 1894 building contract notice.
figures.alt: Manuscript specification for the church at Lyon and Washington.
figures.caption: A named office, a named street, a named minister.

figures.title: Gump’s, San Francisco, period shopfront or interior, 1890s.
figures.alt: Late-nineteenth-century art-goods shop in San Francisco.
figures.caption: Images of the chairs could move from a counter like this. The caption was the danger.

figures.title: A Mission Revival building — a station or school — beside a later “Mission” oak chair, as a comparison plate.
figures.alt: Stucco-and-tile California building paired with a slatted oak chair.
figures.caption: Two uses of one word. Only one of them has friars in it.

figures.title: Binghamton street or a period view of a furniture warehouse district, 1880s.
figures.alt: Upstate New York commercial street in the 1880s.
figures.caption: The brothers sold other men’s chairs here before anyone printed *The Craftsman*.

figures.title: Brandt, Pennsylvania, or a documented Brandt Chair Company mark.
figures.alt: Small-town chair-factory building or a stenciled brand.
figures.caption: The commonplace shop he later named as the start of his feeling for wood.

figures.title: Auburn Prison, exterior, 1890s.
figures.alt: Prison buildings at Auburn, New York.
figures.caption: A furniture workshop on a state contract, 1891–97. Not a guild.

figures.title: Stickley & Simonds, or early Gustave Stickley Company, factory at Eastwood, 1890s.
figures.alt: Wooden factory buildings in a Syracuse suburb.
figures.caption: The 1893 plant is an address before it is a creed.

figures.title: Partnership chair of the 1890s — revival rocker or imitation-bamboo, not a Craftsman slat.
figures.alt: Ornate late-nineteenth-century chair unlike later oak slatwork.
figures.caption: What the partnership knew how to make before New Furniture.

figures.title: New Furniture on the Grand Rapids floor, July 1900, or a period trade-paper cut of the stand.
figures.alt: Exposition aisle with rectilinear oak furniture.
figures.caption: The first Arts and Crafts line was shown in a Michigan trade hall.

figures.title: Poppy table or Celandine table, 1900.
figures.alt: Early Stickley table with a plant-form top or base.
figures.caption: The year included fantastic forms. The later catalog edited them out.

figures.title: Rectilinear New Furniture armchair or stand, 1900–01, with visible joinery.
figures.alt: Early oak chair with exposed mortise-and-tenon.
figures.caption: Wilkinson’s board, and maybe Warner’s, behind a shop mark.

figures.title: *House Beautiful*, October 1900, page on Stickley’s new work.
figures.alt: Magazine page illustrating the Poppy table.
figures.caption: A Chicago monthly captioned the line before *The Craftsman* existed.

figures.title: Tobey Furniture Company, Chicago, period exterior or catalog cover.
figures.alt: Chicago furniture dealer’s building or catalog.
figures.caption: The first national life of the line was a dealer’s word: modern.

figures.title: *The Craftsman*, vol. 1, no. 1, October 1901, cover or title page.
figures.alt: Magazine cover dated October 1901, Eastwood, United Crafts.
figures.caption: Five Morris essays. No price list in the front of the book.

figures.title: October 1901 contents page, Sargent’s five titles visible.
figures.alt: Table of contents naming Morris five times.
figures.caption: A syllabus. The plant is two miles away.

figures.title: Irene Sargent, portrait or a later *Craftsman* masthead with her byline.
figures.alt: Magazine page with Sargent’s name on the lead article.
figures.caption: She wrote the first three numbers alone.
figures.license: PD for a 1901–05 page; confirm for a photograph.

figures.title: A 1904–09 house-plan plate: elevations and a living hall with a settle.
figures.alt: Printed house plan with an inglenook and oak furniture.
figures.caption: The monthly argued a house and a chair as one life.

figures.title: United Crafts or Craftsman Workshops mark, joiner’s compass, *Als ik kan*.
figures.alt: Compass mark with a Flemish motto.
figures.caption: A guild word on a factory product, printed monthly.
figures.license: object photograph CC0 or PD page.

figures.title: December 1916 title page, the last number.
figures.alt: Final *Craftsman* issue dated December 1916.
figures.caption: An argument ran until the imprint was absorbed. A catalog would have stopped with the stock.

figures.title: Eastwood factory buildings, Syracuse suburb, ca. 1900–10.
figures.alt: Wooden factory complex with a rail siding.
figures.caption: A shop number is an address in this plant.

figures.title: Double Manor Hall Seat, shop no. 155, 1900–03.
figures.alt: Long oak hall seat with wrapped arms.
figures.caption: Twenty-three dollars in the early paper. Built by machine and hand.

figures.title: Eastwood paper label, the word Eastwood at the bottom, pencil notes for model and finish.
figures.alt: Paper shop label reading Eastwood.
figures.caption: The suburb wanted its name on the goods.

figures.title: Crouse stables, Syracuse, the local Craftsman Building, after 1900.
figures.alt: Converted stables used as a furniture showroom.
figures.caption: This Craftsman Building is not the later twelve-story one in Manhattan.

figures.title: Quartersawn white oak, ray fleck, on a settle arm or chair seat, preferably a fumed unrestored surface.
figures.alt: Close view of oak fleck on a fumed surface.
figures.caption: The brown of the catalog is often ammonia and tannin, not a wipe of pigment.

figures.title: A catalog plate with shop numbers visible, United Crafts or Craftsman Workshops, 1901–05.
figures.alt: Catalog page of oak furniture with printed numbers.
figures.caption: The dark room was in the rubbing room. The plant printed itself.

figures.title: Gustav Stickley armchair, ca. 1903.
figures.alt: Tall oak armchair with metal-and-wood inlay on the posts and a leather seat.
figures.caption: The museum now files the chair under Stickley and a shop, not under Ellis alone.

figures.title: “Structure and Ornament in the Craftsman Workshops,” *The Craftsman* 5 (January 1904), chair plate.
figures.alt: Magazine photograph of an inlaid oak chair.
figures.caption: The portfolio the market still calls Ellis ran in the month he died.

figures.title: July 1903 *Craftsman* announcement of the new models.
figures.alt: Two-page magazine advertisement for lighter inlaid furniture.
figures.caption: The July notice promised wood inlay. The January plates added pewter and copper.

figures.title: Inlaid armchair, Craftsman Workshops, ca. 1903–04.
figures.alt: Oak armchair with pewter, copper, and fruitwood inlay.
figures.caption: A decal under the armrest is a shop mark. It is not a signature.

figures.title: Harvey Ellis, architectural perspective, midwestern years, as published in *American Architect*.
figures.alt: Signed pen-and-ink perspective of a Richardsonian building.
figures.caption: He was famous as a renderer before anyone paid him to think about a settle.

figures.title: M. H. Baillie Scott or Mackintosh interior with inlaid furniture, for comparison.
figures.alt: English or Glasgow room with inlaid chairs.
figures.caption: The Met calls these cousins. They are not Eastwood employers.

figures.title: “Announcement of the Homebuilders Club,” *The Craftsman*, February 1904, p. 524.
figures.alt: Magazine page offering free working drawings to subscribers.
figures.caption: The club is the moment a chair catalog grew a floor plan.

figures.title: First-floor plan of a Craftsman house with inglenook, 1904–09 plate.
figures.alt: Floor plan showing a fireplace nook with built-in seats.
figures.caption: The settle is drawn as a wall. That is the argument.

figures.title: House No. 79, November 1909, exterior and inglenook note.
figures.alt: Cement house elevation and a caption naming the nook.
figures.caption: By 1909 the magazine could call an eight-room interior “typically Craftsman” and mean the fittings.

figures.title: Syracuse house, Columbus Avenue: inglenook as published in December 1902.
figures.alt: Brick fireplace alcove with a window seat.
figures.caption: Howe walked the rehearsal two years before the club.
figures.license: 1902 plate PD; modern photo rights vary.

figures.title: Built-in sideboard or bookcase in a Craftsman interior plate.
figures.alt: Dining room with a sideboard treated as woodwork.
figures.caption: A sideboard that is a wall cannot be sold twice. The house sells it once.

figures.title: *Craftsman Homes*, 1909, title page or bound plate list.
figures.alt: Title page of the 1909 house book.
figures.caption: The furniture catalogs are a different pile. They share a moral, not an order form.

figures.title: Log house, Craftsman Farms, chestnut trunks and stone, Morris Plains.
figures.alt: Long log house with stone chimneys on a New Jersey rise.
figures.caption: The trunks were cut on the property. The school they were meant to serve did not open.
figures.license: historic PD preferred; museum terms for modern views.

figures.title: *The Craftsman*, December 1908, club-house announcement.
figures.alt: Magazine page promising a club house and spring construction.
figures.caption: “Early in spring” was a caption. The clearing took longer.

figures.title: Living hall of the log house, furnished, a period or early photograph.
figures.alt: Interior of a log living hall with a settle and a table.
figures.caption: A family house, not a campus. The hall still wants a settle.

figures.title: White Cottage, 1910, exterior.
figures.alt: Small cottage on the Craftsman Farms grounds.
figures.caption: The family likely lived here while the logs were still a pile.

figures.title: Site plan or period map of the tract, 1908–17.
figures.alt: Map showing the log house, cottages, and farm buildings.
figures.caption: Six hundred acres, or six hundred fifty. Thirty remain with the buildings.

figures.title: 1917 sale notice or Farny-era photograph of the core.
figures.alt: Printed sale language or an early Farny view of the log house.
figures.caption: Asked one hundred thousand. Sold for sixty. The chestnut did not move.

figures.title: Craftsman Building, 6 East 39th Street, as illustrated in *The Craftsman*, January 1914.
figures.alt: Magazine illustration of a twelve-story midtown loft.
figures.caption: Headquarters for Home Builders. The letterhead address is 39th Street, not 29th.

figures.title: Printed typical floor plan for 5 East 38th / 6 East 39th, from the lease file.
figures.alt: Loft floor plan with two street fronts.
figures.caption: The crash begins as a through-block lease, not as a sermon.

figures.title: Craftsman Restaurant, twelfth floor, period interior or kitchen view.
figures.alt: Dining room or open kitchen on the top floor.
figures.caption: Lunch from Morris Plains, served above the showrooms. Another payroll.

figures.title: *New York Times*, 24 March 1915, bankruptcy notice.
figures.alt: Newspaper paragraph naming Stickley and the adjudication.
figures.caption: The date is firm. The dollar split still wants the page.

figures.title: Model room inside the Craftsman Building, 1913–15.
figures.alt: Furnished Craftsman interior in a loft showroom.
figures.caption: Education meant a room you could walk through and then order.

figures.title: Gimbels advertisement, August 1916, Craftsman stock at 35–50 percent off.
figures.alt: Department-store sale notice for Craftsman Workshops goods.
figures.caption: The corporation’s chairs outlived the corporation’s rent.

figures.title: Onondaga Shops paper label or decal on a Fayetteville chair.
figures.alt: Oval or rectangular paper mark reading Onondaga Shops.
figures.caption: The county comes before Handcraft. It is not Eastwood’s mark.

figures.title: Red Handcraft clamp decal, L. & J.G. Stickley.
figures.alt: Red woodworker’s clamp with the Handcraft name.
figures.caption: A red clamp is not a red compass. The rhyme sold. It also confused.
figures.license: object photo rights vary; 1906–12 decal as object.

figures.title: “The Work of L. & J.G. Stickley” rectangle, ca. 1912.
figures.alt: Red-and-yellow rectangular shopmark naming both brothers.
figures.caption: A sentence that keeps the surname and drops the echo.

figures.title: L. & J.G. Morris chair or settle, marked Handcraft, ca. 1906–12.
figures.alt: Oak reclining chair or settle with a visible Fayetteville mark.
figures.caption: The grammar is American oak. The shop is Fayetteville’s.

figures.title: Onondaga Shops / L. & J.G. catalog page, mid-1900s.
figures.alt: Catalog plate of Mission oak furniture from Fayetteville.
figures.caption: They sold furniture. They did not sell a monthly argument.

figures.title: *Furniture World*, 1918, notice of the Stickley company officers.
figures.alt: Paragraph listing Leopold, Gustav, and J. George as officers.
figures.caption: A notice is not a statute. A year later the older brother is gone.

figures.title: *Quaint Furniture*, Catalogue No. 28, January 1906, cover or title page.
figures.alt: Catalog cover reading Quaint Furniture, Stickley Brothers, Grand Rapids.
figures.caption: The title page names a city and an English adjective. Not a magazine.

figures.title: Brass Quaint Furniture tag, Art Nouveau cartouche.
figures.alt: Metal plate stamped Quaint Furniture.
figures.caption: Hardware a warehouse can read. Not a joiner’s compass.

figures.title: Quaint Mission armchair or settle, ca. 1904–10, tagged.
figures.alt: Oak slat armchair with a Stickley Brothers tag.
figures.caption: The slat is American. The plant is Michigan’s.

figures.title: Catalogue No. 38, 1912, mahogany section or a figured-mahogany plate.
figures.alt: Catalog page of Quaint furniture in mahogany.
figures.caption: A Grand Rapids Mission line could be priced in more than one wood.

figures.title: 1 January 1912 price list keyed to Catalogue No. 38.
figures.alt: Printed price list dated January 1, 1912.
figures.caption: Numbers next to plates. The range is the evidence.

figures.title: Bewdley or other English-looking Stickley Brothers case with floral inlay, ca. 1902.
figures.alt: Inlaid case with an English shop silhouette.
figures.caption: Bewdley is a place-name. The case was made in Grand Rapids.

figures.title: Craftsman Workshops catalog page and L. & J.G. Handcraft catalog page, same furniture type, facing.
figures.alt: Two catalog plates of oak settles or Morris chairs.
figures.caption: The slats agree. The shop numbers do not.

figures.title: Eastwood price list, a dated year, Morris chair or settle line.
figures.alt: Printed prices keyed to shop numbers.
figures.caption: A list is a contract. The moral language is optional.

figures.title: Handcraft price list or numbered catalog, same season if possible.
figures.alt: Fayetteville prices for comparable forms.
figures.caption: Competition is arithmetic before it is a story.

figures.title: *Furniture World*, 1918, officers’ notice.
figures.alt: Paragraph naming Leopold, Gustav, and J. George.
figures.caption: President, vice president, treasurer. A year later, two officers.

figures.title: Combined or transitional shopmark sometimes called Associated Cabinetmakers, if a documented example exists.
figures.alt: Circular mark joining clamp and compass language.
figures.caption: A rare decal is not a statute. Photograph it, then read the minutes.

figures.title: Roycroft Inn, South Grove Street, East Aurora, a historic view, ca. 1905–15.
figures.alt: Stone-and-timber inn facing a village street.
figures.caption: Guests came for the press. The Inn is what you do with guests.

figures.title: Roycroft Print Shop, 1901 building, exterior.
figures.alt: Stone print shop across from the Inn.
figures.caption: 1901. Garcia’s money in the walls.

figures.title: *The Philistine*, an 1895–1900 cover, or the *Message to Garcia* booklet.
figures.alt: Little-magazine cover or pamphlet title page.
figures.caption: The campus begins as type. The chairs come later.

figures.title: Campus plan or period bird’s-eye of South Grove and Main.
figures.alt: Map of print shop, inn, chapel, copper shop, furniture shop.
figures.caption: A village industry with paths. Not a Syracuse suburb.

figures.title: Elbert Hubbard at East Aurora, a dated photograph.
figures.alt: Hubbard on the campus, identifiable by period dress.
figures.caption: The character sold the campus. The character is not a shop drawing.

figures.title: *Lusitania* sailing notice or a 1915 newspaper naming the Hubbards among the lost.
figures.alt: Period news paragraph.
figures.caption: 7 May 1915. The press lost its founder. The benches did not sink.

figures.title: Orb-and-cross carved on a Roycroft furniture rail, ca. 1906–10.
figures.alt: Carved circle, double-barred cross, and R on an oak rail.
figures.caption: A printer’s colophon doing sales work on a chair.

figures.title: Magazine pedestal, model 080, quartersawn white oak, ca. 1910.
figures.alt: Tall oak pedestal with carved Roycroft devices.
figures.caption: A form the campus needed because it sold books.

figures.title: Thirty-third-degree bookcase, model 86, ca. 1905–06.
figures.alt: Oak bookcase with Gothic glass and a carved shopmark.
figures.caption: The high end of the range. The mark does not make every cousin its equal.

figures.title: Hammered copper tray or muffin dish, orb-and-cross punch, ca. 1906–12.
figures.alt: Copper dish with a punched R-in-orb on the underside.
figures.caption: The same brand in a metal a household could mail.

figures.title: *Roycroft Handmade Furniture*, 1912, a catalog page of chairs or pedestals.
figures.alt: Catalog plate with model numbers and oak furniture.
figures.caption: Eighty-plus designs. A campus list, not a Syracuse shop-number system.

figures.title: Grove Park Inn interior, Asheville, or a period photograph of Roycroft furnishings in the hotel, 1913 or after.
figures.alt: Hotel room or lobby furnished with rectilinear oak and copper lighting.
figures.caption: A hotel order is a production problem. The mark still wanted to be on the goods.

figures.title: Leaded window, Roycroft Inn, attributed to Dard Hunter, 1906.
figures.alt: Leaded-glass window with a central flower in a grid of colored squares.
figures.caption: The flower is the argument. The chair shop is a different room.

figures.title: Dard Hunter, *Design for a three-part window in the style of Mackintosh*, ca. 1909–11.
figures.alt: Three narrow watercolor elevations for a leaded window.
figures.caption: A graphic mind thinking in lead, not in through-tenons.

figures.title: Electrolier for the Roycroft Inn dining room, 1909–10.
figures.alt: Three hanging leaded shades in green and lavender under a copper cap.
figures.caption: Square voids and a beam hook. Vienna after the magazine, then after the honeymoon.

figures.title: Title page by Hunter for a Roycroft book, 1905.
figures.alt: Printed title page with Hunter initials and geometry.
figures.caption: He was hired to design books. The glass was an expansion of that job.

figures.title: *My Life with Paper*, Alfred A. Knopf, 1958, title page or jacket.
figures.alt: 1958 autobiography title page naming Dard Hunter and Knopf.
figures.caption: The furniture decade became a preface. He wrote the book as a papermaker.
figures.license: jacket copyright; title-page photograph for study.

figures.title: Roycroft armchair with orb-and-cross, oak, about 1906.
figures.alt: Oak side chair with a carved orb-and-cross on the front rail.
figures.caption: The campus brand on a chair. Hunter’s name does not belong on the rail unless the document says so.

figures.title: Charles Rohlfs, revolving fall-front desk from the Graceful Writing Set, ca. 1899.
figures.alt: Tall oak desk with flame finials and a cabinet that swivels on a footed base.
figures.caption: It turns. The slat never arrives.

figures.title: Desk chair from the Rohlfs house, ca. 1898–99.
figures.alt: Narrow oak chair with a carved splat and a high back.
figures.caption: Label “#4 Carved Desk Chair.” Sculpture that permits sitting.

figures.title: Hall chair from the Graceful Writing Set, 1904 example.
figures.alt: Tall fretted oak side chair with a pierced back.
figures.caption: The only chair he repeated in any number. Still not a Mission type.

figures.title: *House Beautiful*, January 1900, page with Rohlfs furniture.
figures.alt: Magazine page illustrating Rohlfs oak.
figures.caption: Charlotte Moffitt’s article is the first published account of the shop.

figures.title: Pan-American Exposition, Buffalo, 1901, a Rohlfs chair or installation photograph.
figures.alt: Carved oak chair dated 1901, or a period fair interior.
figures.caption: Same grounds as McHugh’s loan. A different grammar.

figures.title: Shop mark: R imposed on a bow saw, impressed in oak.
figures.alt: Close-up of a branded R over a saw outline.
figures.caption: Not a red decal. Not an orb-and-cross. A saw.

figures.title: Charles P. Limbert Co., library table, model 146, ca. 1910.
figures.alt: Oval oak table with geometric cutouts in plank sides and a lower shelf.
figures.caption: Page 17 of the Holland Dutch booklet. The inside corners are slightly round.
figures.license: museum or owner permission; catalog cut PD.

figures.title: Brand on the underside: *Made in Grand Rapids and Holland*.
figures.alt: Burned shopmark naming Limbert, Grand Rapids, and Holland.
figures.caption: A double address after 1906. The machinery had moved. The older city stayed on the iron.

figures.title: Catalog page, *Limbert’s Holland Dutch Arts and Crafts Furniture*, ca. 1910.
figures.alt: Trade-catalog page of oak tables and copy invoking Dutch origins.
figures.caption: The plant’s own word was Dutch, not Japanese.

figures.title: Limbert tabouret with curved plank supports, 1905–15.
figures.alt: Small oak stand with curved legs unlike a standard Mission angle.
figures.caption: The line was larger than the oval trophy.

figures.title: Library table with pull-out writing surface, 1905–15.
figures.alt: Rectangular oak library table with a hinged writing leaf.
figures.caption: A factory inventing uses, not only voids.

figures.title: Period view of the Holland, Michigan, plant or a Grand Rapids showroom interior.
figures.alt: Brick factory or showroom with oak furniture in racks.
figures.caption: Two hundred to two hundred fifty people, not a tea room.

figures.title: Paper label or decal, *Lifetime Furniture / Grand Rapids Bookcase & Chair Co.*
figures.alt: Black-and-white paper label naming Lifetime and the Hastings company.
figures.caption: The line is Lifetime. The factory is a Grand Rapids name in a Hastings town.
figures.license: object photograph; label is a historic trademark.

figures.title: Bookcase, model 7604, ca. 1910–12.
figures.alt: Wide oak bookcase with three glass doors and copper hardware.
figures.caption: A factory number, a decal, a middle price.

figures.title: Title page or plate from *Life-Time Furniture: The Cloister Styles*, ca. 1911.
figures.alt: Catalog page of heavy oak settees and tables.
figures.caption: Two hundred seventy-two items. Not a studio.

figures.title: Catalog ornament: monks or a mission-church cut.
figures.alt: Line drawing of monks or a Southwestern church used to sell oak.
figures.caption: Cloister as a mood. The California word, rented again.

figures.title: Lifetime settle, oak, ca. 1911.
figures.alt: Heavy oak settle with straight posts and a leather or wood seat.
figures.caption: Thicker than Ellis-period Craftsman. Aimed at a different invoice.

figures.title: Pál Horti / Shop of the Crafters, China Cabinet No. 326, ca. 1905.
figures.alt: Tall oak china cabinet with glass doors and contrasting wood inlay.
figures.caption: A museum number and a Hungarian name. Start here.

figures.title: Gold paper label with lantern, Oscar Onken Co., Cincinnati.
figures.alt: Gold label reading Shop of the Crafters at Cincinnati.
figures.caption: Sole owners. Not a guild minutes book.

figures.title: Shop of the Crafters catalog, 1906, Horti page or a Viennese room setting.
figures.alt: Catalog page naming Professor Paul Horti or showing a furnished room.
figures.caption: St. Louis copy, Cincinnati prices.

figures.title: Inlaid desk or table, Shop of the Crafters, ca. 1906.
figures.alt: Oak desk with colored-wood inlay on the drawer faces.
figures.caption: Mission lines, European surface.

figures.title: *The Lantern*, vol. 1, no. 1, cover or masthead.
figures.alt: Cover of the shop’s promotional magazine.
figures.caption: A house organ, not *The Craftsman*.

figures.title: Louisiana Purchase Exposition, 1904, Hungarian or Austrian interior (period photograph).
figures.alt: World’s-fair room with Central European furniture.
figures.caption: The hiring scene, if the catalog is telling a usable truth.

figures.title: Settle or bench with carved floral panel, White Pines / Byrdcliffe shop, ca. 1904.
figures.alt: Low oak settle with a carved leaf panel in the back rail.
figures.caption: Sitting furniture for a house named after trees. Not a catalog number.

figures.title: Byrdcliffe linen press, sassafras doors by Edna Walker, ca. 1904.
figures.alt: Green-stained oak cabinet with carved sassafras leaves on the doors.
figures.caption: The museum object. Walker’s leaves, a boxy case, a two-year shop.

figures.title: Outline drawing of the sassafras linen press, 1904.
figures.alt: Pencil elevation of a cabinet with leaf panels.
figures.caption: Shop paper. The fight over who drew the case is still open.

figures.title: Lily chair, splat designed by Zulma Steele, ca. 1904.
figures.alt: Side chair with a painted or carved lily on the splat.
figures.caption: The colony’s plant, on a back a guest could lean against.

figures.title: White Pines, exterior or a Beals interior, ca. 1903–07.
figures.alt: Dark-sided Arts and Crafts house with blue-trimmed windows, or a hall with oak seating.
figures.caption: The house that was supposed to be a factory’s showroom and became a colony’s.

figures.title: Zulma Steele and Edna Walker, a working drawing from Winterthur.
figures.alt: Furniture cartoon with a floral panel and shop dimensions.
figures.caption: Pratt, Dow, the Angelus, and the leaves later given to men in the room.

figures.title: Rose Valley Shops, library table, 1904.
figures.alt: Dark oak trestle table with Gothic carved ends and visible butterfly keys.
figures.caption: Crozer’s table, April 1904, fifty dollars. The pins come out.

figures.title: Detail of a carved figural pin and a butterfly key.
figures.alt: Close-up of a carved oak pin through a trestle and a dovetail key in the top.
figures.caption: Loose construction. Honesty as hardware.

figures.title: Rose Valley side chair with Gothic tracery splat, 1901–06.
figures.alt: Oak side chair with lancets cut in the back like an empty window.
figures.caption: The common form, rarely a matched set.

figures.title: *The Artsman* 1, no. 1 (October 1903), table drawing.
figures.alt: Magazine page with a small trestle table and Rose Valley copy.
figures.caption: A mill-village monthly, not *The Craftsman*.

figures.title: The old mill on Ridley Creek, or Tower House, ca. 1903–15.
figures.alt: Stone mill or a small studio house in a Pennsylvania creek valley.
figures.caption: A wrecked textile site, not a shipped Cotswold.

figures.title: Rose Valley brand: rose, V, buckled belt.
figures.alt: Branded mark with a rose and a V inside a belted circle.
figures.caption: Fellowship as a stamp. Not every shop piece has it.

figures.title: Arturo Bandini House, courtyard or veranda, 1903, historic photograph.
figures.alt: U-shaped wooden house around a courtyard with a fountain and verandas.
figures.caption: The California plan before the teak hall. Demolished 1961.

figures.title: Bandini interior, redwood board-and-batten, period photograph.
figures.alt: Simple paneled room with beams and a stone fireplace.
figures.caption: Not yet the Gamble dining room. Built-in wood, barn language.

figures.title: Edward S. Morse, *Japanese Homes and Their Surroundings*, 1886, a plate of posts on stones.
figures.alt: Book illustration of a Japanese veranda post resting on a stone.
figures.caption: Charles bought the book in 1903 and changed the Bandini drawings.

figures.title: Desk for the Adelaide Tichenor house, Long Beach, ca. 1904.
figures.alt: Ash fall-front desk with slab sides and butterfly splines.
figures.caption: Stickley’s desk grammar on a Long Beach job. The Hall mahogany has not arrived.

figures.title: Bureau for the Jennie Reeve house, Long Beach, ca. 1904.
figures.alt: Oak bureau with projecting through-tenons.
figures.caption: Visible joinery, thick stock. A Mission reader will misfile it.

figures.title: Dining armchair for the Laurabelle A. Robinson house, 1906.
figures.alt: Armchair whose stretcher rises in a cloud-lift curve.
figures.caption: The motif arrives before the Gambles do.

figures.title: Ho-o-den, World’s Columbian Exposition, Chicago, 1893.
figures.alt: Wooden Japanese pavilion at the Chicago fair.
figures.caption: A train stop, not yet a furniture style.

figures.title: Dining table, Gamble House, 1908.
figures.alt: Mahogany dining table with lobed corners and an ebony-detailed base.
figures.caption: Tsuba corners, not a Mission chamfer. The wood is not oak.

figures.title: Dining chairs at the table, 1908–09.
figures.alt: Dining chairs with cloud-lift rails and square ebony pegs.
figures.caption: Site chairs for this room. A slat suite was for any freight door.

figures.title: Cloud-lift rail and ebony peg, dining chair or table base.
figures.alt: Close view of a raised rail and a square ebony peg in mahogany.
figures.caption: The lift is cut in the rail. The peg is a period, not an Eastwood pin.

figures.title: Built-in dining sideboard and rose leaded screen.
figures.alt: Built-in sideboard with a rose-patterned glass screen above.
figures.caption: The table is not a loose suite. The wall was designed with it.

figures.title: Dining-room ceiling fixture, 1908.
figures.alt: Hanging canopy fixture with lobed corners over a dining table.
figures.caption: Leather straps and a tsuba outline. Not a catalog electrolier.

figures.title: Robinson House dining host chair, for the Huntington comparison.
figures.alt: Mahogany dining armchair from another Pasadena house of the same years.
figures.caption: A cousin at the Huntington. Not David and Mary’s table. Keep the addresses apart.

figures.title: Arm detail, Blacker House living-room armchair, 1908–09.
figures.alt: Mahogany chair arm with a cloud-lift profile and a square ebony peg in the post.
figures.caption: The lift is cut in the rail. The peg is a period, not a pin.

figures.title: X-ray of the Blacker armchair arm-to-post joint.
figures.alt: Radiograph showing a tenon, a deep mortise, and plugs in their own holes.
figures.caption: Cooke’s film is the shop practice the drawing does not confess.

figures.title: Robinson House dining host chair.
figures.alt: Mahogany dining armchair with softened edges and no Mission slat.
figures.caption: The Huntington still prints 1905–06. Cooke argues 1907. The chair can bear both dates.

figures.title: Gamble House master-bedroom chiffonier, drawer corner.
figures.alt: Finger-jointed drawer with a modeled ebony plug over a screw.
figures.caption: Machine fingers, hand-modeled plug. The shop spent time where the hand would land.

figures.title: South Raymond shop, or the later Hall Manufacturing interior.
figures.alt: A long mill interior with saws and stacked stock.
figures.caption: A one-story carpentry shop, not a guild romance.

figures.title: Cloud-lift crest, Gamble House living-room rocker.
figures.alt: Oak or mahogany rocker crest with a bold double-arc lift.
figures.caption: Same vocabulary, different volume. The lift is not a transferred decal.

figures.title: Robie House dining side chair, oak, 1908–10.
figures.alt: Very tall oak side chair with a slatted back and a small seat pad.
figures.caption: Fifty-two inches of slat. Hanks measured the wall.

figures.title: Dining table and chairs in situ, Robie House, period photograph.
figures.alt: A long dining table with lamp piers, ringed by high-back chairs.
figures.caption: The lamps pull in. The backs stop the room.

figures.title: Wright Home and Studio dining chairs, Oak Park, 1895.
figures.alt: High-back oak dining chairs with wooden spheres at the stiles.
figures.caption: The wall is already here. Robie edits the spheres away.
figures.license: confirm Trust rights; historic PD if a period plate exists.

figures.title: Willits House dining chair.
figures.alt: Stained oak high-back chair, 1902.
figures.caption: Same idea, earlier house, a museum number in London.

figures.title: Dana House dining room, Springfield, looking toward the table.
figures.alt: A barrel-vaulted dining room with mixed-height chairs and art glass.
figures.caption: Dana is the other set. It is not this set.

figures.title: Robie living-dining interior from the 1910 portfolio, or a measured drawing of the chair.
figures.alt: A plate showing the long horizontal room and the dining enclosure.
figures.caption: Wright’s preface refused to split the chair from the house.

figures.title: Frank Lloyd Wright, spindle cube chair, 1902–06.
figures.alt: Cubic armchair of thin vertical spindles, open to light.
figures.caption: Twenty-nine inches of poplar. A studio chair, not a catalog page.

figures.title: Gustav Stickley slat armchair, oak, about 1904–07.
figures.alt: Oak armchair with five wide back slats and a leather seat.
figures.caption: A shop number is already a different kind of name.
figures.license: Met CC0 if a slat example is CC0; otherwise museum terms.

figures.title: L. & J.G. Stickley “Prairie” cube or settle, catalog plate, about 1910.
figures.alt: Catalog cut of a massive cube chair with wide arms.
figures.caption: Fayetteville could borrow the word. It could not borrow the house.

figures.title: Purcell and Elmslie furniture in a documented interior, or the Elmslie clock.
figures.alt: A Prairie interior with custom chairs or a geometric clock.
figures.caption: Architectural time. No freight crate to a retailer.

figures.title: Grand Rapids “Mission” suite cut, about 1906–10.
figures.alt: A matching oak parlor suite in a trade-paper plate.
figures.caption: This is what Mission meant when it meant a line.

figures.title: End-grain of a quartersawn white-oak arm or through-tenon.
figures.alt: Close view of oak end-grain with pale radial lines meeting a dark face.
figures.caption: The ray in cross-section. Turn the arm and it becomes fleck.

figures.title: Face of a quartersawn white-oak rail showing flake.
figures.alt: Horizontal oak rail with glossy medullary-ray patches.
figures.caption: The photograph the catalogs were already selling.

figures.title: Diagram of plainsawn versus quartersawn log breakdown.
figures.alt: Two log diagrams, rings and rays oriented differently to the board face.
figures.caption: Quartersawn is a geometry. It wastes the log on purpose.

figures.title: Plainsawn oak chair rail beside a quartersawn rail, same finish if possible.
figures.alt: Two oak rails, one cupping and quiet of flake, one flat and flecked.
figures.caption: The cheap cut is not a moral failure. It is a different board.

figures.title: *The Craftsman* or Eastwood catalog page in which the fleck is visible in halftone.
figures.alt: Catalog photograph of a settle or armchair with visible ray figure.
figures.caption: A customer who could not name a ray could still want one.

figures.title: Wedged or pinned through-tenon on a settle arm.
figures.alt: Oak post with a tenon end and a wedge or pin proud of the surface.
figures.caption: The arm does not die in the post. You can put a fingernail on the wedge.
figures.license: museum CC0 or PD dealer-archive photograph with rights cleared.

figures.title: Catalog D, settle no. 210, page or plate.
figures.alt: Catalog photograph of a long oak settle with projecting tenons.
figures.caption: Eastwood called the pins decoration. They were also pins.

figures.title: False through-tenon or applied end-grain plug on a factory Mission armchair.
figures.alt: A post with a rectangular “tenon” that does not emerge from a rail.
figures.caption: Sham is a caption. The rail never arrived.

figures.title: Early Stickley Morris chair, shop 2342, front-post through-tenons.
figures.alt: Reclining oak armchair with heavy tenons coming through the front legs.
figures.caption: Thick, a little proud, still a factory — and still a through joint.

figures.title: Hall shop ebony pegs on a Greene and Greene rail (contrast).
figures.alt: Square ebony plugs on mahogany, no oak tenon showing.
figures.caption: A different picture of structure. Not a religion. Not Eastwood.

figures.title: Pair of quartersawn white-oak samples, fumed historic surface versus pigment-stained surface.
figures.alt: Two oak rectangles, one even cool brown, one with pale rays and dark pores.
figures.caption: Same cut, two colors. The ray tells you which is which.

figures.title: Gustav Stickley armchair, documented original film, about 1904.
figures.alt: Dark oak armchair whose fleck is close in tone to the ground.
figures.caption: Texture, not outline. The 1904 brown as a surface you can still find.

figures.title: The same model, later refinished, if a documented pair exists; or a 1980s “restored” settle.
figures.alt: An oak settle with high-contrast flake and a thick modern sheen.
figures.caption: The story was stripped. The brown that replaced it is another year.

figures.title: *The Craftsman*, October 1905, opening of the oak-finish essay (title and first sentences only).
figures.alt: Magazine page dated October 1905 with Stickley’s byline.
figures.caption: He published a household paragraph. He said the factory was different.

figures.title: Catalog finish names, Craftsman Workshops, about 1906–12.
figures.alt: Catalog type listing oak finishes and prices for leather or canvas.
figures.caption: By the time the names multiply, dye is already in the plant.

figures.title: Gustav Stickley reclining armchair, shop no. 2342, c. 1902–04.
figures.alt: Heavy oak recliner with five back slats and through-tenons in the front posts.
figures.caption: The shop number is the American name. Morris did not draw it.
figures.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia contributor photograph of museum object)

figures.title: Decal under the left arm, 2342.
figures.alt: Red joiner’s-compass decal on oak.
figures.caption: Authorship as a sticker, not as a Sussex letter.

figures.title: Philip Webb / Morris & Co. adjustable-back armchair.
figures.alt: Ebonized or oak English recliner with bobbin turning and a loose cushion.
figures.caption: Taylor’s sketch, Webb’s chair, a fabric the American version usually refuses.

figures.title: Stickley shop no. 369, spindle drop-arm Morris.
figures.alt: Oak recliner with spindle sides and slanting arms.
figures.caption: Same type, later grammar. Light comes through the sides.

figures.title: Morris & Co. catalog page, c. 1912, still listing the adjustable chair.
figures.alt: English catalog cut of the Morris adjustable-back chair with cover options.
figures.caption: Still in print in London after Eastwood had numbered its own.

figures.title: Grand Rapids or Sears “Morris chair” cut, c. 1908.
figures.alt: A cheap oak recliner in a trade cut.
figures.caption: Once the type was public, the letter in the V&A was optional.

figures.title: L. & J.G. Stickley drop-arm settle, shop no. 263.
figures.alt: Long oak settle with slanting arms, slatted back, leather cushion.
figures.caption: The arms will drop. The piece is still a bench.

figures.title: The same type, arms down, or a detail of the arm pivot.
figures.alt: Settle with arms lowered to the seat line.
figures.caption: A nap without a parlor word.

figures.title: Gustav Stickley even-arm settle, shop no. 208.
figures.alt: Even-arm oak settle, slats, tacked leather.
figures.caption: Eastwood’s hall bench when the arms stay put.

figures.title: Catalog D, settle no. 210, with the hide sentence if the plate includes it.
figures.alt: Very long oak settle in a catalog photograph.
figures.caption: Eighty-four inches. “Recline at full length.” Still not a sofa.

figures.title: Tack line and leather edge on a hall settle.
figures.alt: Close view of metal tacks along a leather cushion on an oak rail.
figures.caption: Fasteners as a dotted line. Hidden staples would be a different grammar.

figures.title: *The Craftsman* living-hall plate with a settle at the fire, 1904–09.
figures.alt: Interior perspective of a living hall with a high-backed bench and chimney.
figures.caption: The room the settle was priced for. A parlor would have wanted a sofa.

figures.title: Gustav Stickley spindle cube, shop no. 391, c. 1905–09.
figures.alt: Cubic oak armchair with a grid of spindles on three sides.
figures.caption: Light comes through. The catalog sold a cage.

figures.title: Gustav Stickley slat armchair, oak, about 1905.
figures.alt: Oak armchair with wide vertical slats and a leather seat.
figures.caption: Light stops. The fleck has a billboard.

figures.title: The two chairs photographed together, or their shadows on a floor.
figures.alt: Spindle cube and slat armchair side by side, or striped shadow versus block shadow.
figures.caption: Same plant. Two jobs. The floor can tell them apart.

figures.title: Wright spindle cube, Art Institute of Chicago 2007.79.
figures.alt: Open cubic chair of thin spindles.
figures.caption: Prairie air, not a Mission plane. Poplar, not the catalog oak.

figures.title: Stickley spindle Morris, shop no. 369, side view.
figures.alt: Reclining chair with spindle sides and an adjustable back.
figures.caption: The plant put air on a recliner too. The slat armchair remained the house brand.

figures.title: Grand Rapids “Mission” parlor suite, trade-paper cut.
figures.alt: Catalog-style drawing of a matching oak davenport, chairs, and table.
figures.caption: The suite is the factory’s unit. The caption is the argument.

figures.title: *The Furniture Record* masthead or a 1912 bound volume opened to a Mission plate.
figures.alt: Trade magazine page naming Grand Rapids.
figures.caption: Buyers read this, not *The Craftsman*.

figures.title: Stickley Brothers, *Quaint Furniture*, Catalogue No. 30, 1908, a room page.
figures.alt: Catalog page offering to furnish a hall or dining room in oak.
figures.caption: Albert’s plant sold a complete school of design. Mission was the popular name for the school.

figures.title: Grand Rapids Furniture Exposition, sample-room interior or a buyer’s order book, about 1910.
figures.alt: Crowded showroom of factory samples.
figures.caption: Knockoff speed is a market calendar, not a mood.

figures.title: Photograph or notice of the 1911 furniture strike.
figures.alt: Furniture workers on a Grand Rapids street, 1911.
figures.caption: The *Record* printed labor as well as suites.

figures.title: Factory Mission armchair, paper label or no mark, next to a documented Eastwood slat chair.
figures.alt: Two oak armchairs of similar silhouette, different marks.
figures.caption: The silhouettes agree more than the sentences do.

figures.title: Larkin Company, February 1916, Three-Piece Mission Suite page.
figures.alt: Catalog cuts of a slat chair, settee, and rocker with coupon prices.
figures.caption: The suite is given with soap. The weights are the other price.

figures.title: Larkin Mission-style library table, quarter-sawed oak, knocked down.
figures.alt: Oak library table with square legs and a lower shelf.
figures.caption: Forty-four by twenty-eight, ninety-eight pounds, from a factory that was not Buffalo.

figures.title: Sears, Roebuck, Catalog No. 124, Spring 1912, a Mission furniture page.
figures.alt: Sears catalog page of slatted oak chairs or a parlor suite.
figures.caption: The look sold among stoves and shoes. Cite the page when the scan is open.

figures.title: Come-Packt Furniture Company, Catalogue H, 1913, cover or a knockdown plate.
figures.alt: Mail-order catalog offering Mission oak to assemble at home.
figures.caption: The name is the instruction: come packed.
figures.license: Met terms; 1913 PD for the page.

figures.title: A Larkin Chautauqua desk, oak, drop front.
figures.alt: Drop-front oak desk with square posts.
figures.caption: The desk that still gets recognized in a small-town parlor.

figures.title: A knockdown crate stencil or a freight bill for household furniture, about 1910–16.
figures.alt: Stenciled crate or printed freight table.
figures.caption: Mail-order Mission begins as empty air you refuse to pay for.

figures.title: L. & J.G. Stickley Early American advertisement, *House and Garden*, 1920s.
figures.alt: Advertisement for maple or cherry Colonial furniture from Fayetteville.
figures.caption: The same firm that had sold Handcraft oak now sold the early 1700s.
figures.license: public domain if pre-1930; confirm later 1920s.

figures.title: A leftover Mission oak settle or rocker in a 1920s interior, or a remainder-sale notice.
figures.alt: Dark oak slat furniture standing apart from lighter Colonial pieces.
figures.caption: The brown did not vanish on a calendar date. It was marked down.

figures.title: Notice or petition matter of the 24 March 1915 bankruptcy.
figures.alt: Legal or newspaper text naming Gustav Stickley, bankrupt.
figures.caption: A court can finish a taste. The date is not a mood.

figures.title: *The Craftsman*, December 1916, cover or last editorial page.
figures.alt: Final magazine issue dated December 1916.
figures.caption: The monthly argument stops. The leftover oak does not.

figures.title: Chromewald or early revival Stickley piece, about 1916–18.
figures.alt: Furniture with a historicizing finish unlike fumed Mission oak.
figures.caption: Even Eastwood reached backward before the magazine died.

figures.title: 1920s Colonial Revival dining room in maple or mahogany, shelter-magazine plate.
figures.alt: Bright wood dining room with turned legs and no slatted oak.
figures.caption: The wood shift is the taste shift. Mahogany had always known how to wait.

figures.title: *The Magazine Antiques*, May 1977, opening page of Bohdan and Volpe, “The furniture of Gustav Stickley.”
figures.alt: 1977 magazine article title naming Gustav Stickley.
figures.caption: A monthly that preferred Salem was willing to treat Eastwood as antiques.
figures.license: magazine terms; fair-use captioning for scholarship.

figures.title: Clark, *The Arts and Crafts Movement in America 1876–1916*, 1972, cover or a Stickley plate.
figures.alt: 1972 exhibition catalog cover.
figures.caption: October 1972. The movement becomes a thing a collector can study.

figures.title: Jordan-Volpe Gallery, 457 West Broadway, a 1970s installation or a period advertisement.
figures.alt: SoHo room of oak desks and copper pulls.
figures.caption: The collector market has an address.

figures.title: David Cathers, *Furniture of the American Arts and Crafts Movement*, 1981, title page or a marked chair plate.
figures.alt: 1981 book identifying Stickley and Roycroft oak.
figures.caption: Identification for a desk. Not a 1904 price list.

figures.title: A Streisand-era newspaper headline on a Stickley sale, 1988.
figures.alt: Headline pairing a celebrity name with Mission oak.
figures.caption: The useful fact is that a sideboard could be news. Verify the hammer in the catalog.

figures.title: A 1980s price-guide spread, Johnson or equivalent, Mission oak entries.
figures.alt: Dollar columns next to oak rockers and settles.
figures.caption: Evidence of the market that printed it. Not evidence of Eastwood.

figures.title: L. & J.G. Stickley Mission Oak Collection shopmark, 1989, burned and dated.
figures.alt: Burned shopmark and a cabinetmaker’s date on new oak.
figures.caption: The tag is the argument. This is a reissue, not a barn find.
figures.license: object photograph with permission; catalog PD not applicable (1989).

figures.title: 1989 Mission Oak Collection catalog, a chair plate with an old shop number and a new date.
figures.alt: Catalog page of a slat armchair numbered as in an early list.
figures.caption: The old number is a drawing. The date is the object.

figures.title: *Chicago Tribune*, 30 April 1989, the reproduction article.
figures.alt: 1989 headline on Mission oak put back into production.
figures.caption: The auction rooms had already made the line visible.
figures.license: newspaper terms; quote as dated type.

figures.title: A counterfeit or “improved” Craftsman mark beside a documented Eastwood mark.
figures.alt: Two marks, one true, one later.
figures.caption: A fake is a name the shop did not give.

figures.title: Three slat armchairs: a documented early Stickley, a dated 1989 reissue, an unmarked contemporary chair in the same grammar.
figures.alt: Three oak armchairs of similar silhouette, different marks and dates.
figures.caption: The through-tenon can be shared. Authorship cannot.

figures.title: Postcard, Bradley Lumber Company of Arkansas, mill and factories, Warren.
figures.alt: Mill yard and stacks of lumber among trees, Warren, Arkansas.
figures.caption: The stack is furniture stock. The caption is a freight bill.

figures.title: End grain of quartersawn white oak, ray fleck visible.
figures.alt: Oak end grain showing medullary rays.
figures.caption: A mill that will still quarter the log is making the expensive board on purpose.
figures.license: CC0 if a museum board; otherwise confirm.

figures.title: A through-tenon on a settle arm, shop contemporary or historic.
figures.alt: Keyed or pinned tenon coming through a post.
figures.caption: The joint outlasted the fashion. It is a method, not a brand.

figures.title: A measured catalog plate — Craftsman, Quaint, Larkin, or 1989 — beside a shop drawing.
figures.alt: Numbered furniture drawing next to a later measured sheet.
figures.caption: Continuity is a dimension, not a mood.
figures.license: PD for the old page; confirm the new.

figures.title: Leftover Mission oak still in a bungalow or a small-town library.
figures.alt: Dark slatted settle in a room that was never redesigned.
figures.caption: Too sturdy for the 1920s to destroy. No one in the room is thinking about Sargent.

figures.title: Mixed rail car or lumber-yard bill, southern hardwood, early twentieth century.
figures.alt: Freight document naming oak and furniture stock.
figures.caption: The board can be shipped. The life of work cannot.
